title: Temporal Generalization: A Reality Check
topic: General Machine Learning->Transfer, Multitask and Meta-learning
claim: Models trained once degrade as data drifts over time, motivating a framework that estimates future parameters from past training stages.
layout: 2 panels, left plot then right staircase diagram, time on x-axis
description: The left panel is a line plot of cumulative average perplexity against time, from 2012-03 to 2016-09. A red solid line for a stale model θ0 climbs steadily toward 1.8. A green dashed line for a monthly updated model θt climbs more slowly and ends near 1.6. The gap between them widens, and light shaded bands show variance. The right panel is a schematic with stages S1, S2, ..., St stacked on the y-axis and time on the x-axis. At each stage an orange training box f_θ is fed data D and passes parameters up and to the right to the next stage. Blue evaluation boxes with estimated parameters θ̃ sit to the right of a dashed vertical divider and are fed future data D. A legend marks orange as Training and blue as Evaluation.
caption: (Left) Performance degrades over time. The widening performance gap between a stale model trained once in January 2012 (red) and a monthly updated model (green) illustrates the decay in performance over time. The evaluation was conducted using data from March 2012 onward. (Right) Temporal generalization framework. Across sequential learning stages (St on the y-axis), a model fθt is trained on data Dt (orange) initialized with θt−1 from the previous stage. This generates a sequence of historical parameters. This sequence is used to estimate future parameters eθt+δ, which are used to evaluate future data (blue) Dt+δ for δ > 0 (x-axis).
abstract: Machine learning (ML) models often struggle to maintain performance under distribution shifts, leading to inaccurate predictions on unseen future data. In this work, we investigate whether and under what conditions models can achieve such a generalization when relying solely on past data. We explore two primary approaches: convex combinations of past model parameters (\emph{parameter interpolation}) and explicit extrapolation beyond the convex hull of past parameters (\emph{parameter extrapolation}). We benchmark several methods within these categories on a diverse set of temporal tasks, including language modeling, news summarization, news tag prediction, academic paper categorization, satellite image-based land use classification over time, and historical yearbook photo gender prediction. Our empirical findings show that none of the evaluated methods consistently outperforms the simple baseline of using the latest available model parameters in all scenarios. In the absence of access to future data or robust assumptions about the underlying data-generating process, these results underscore the inherent difficulties of generalizing and extrapolating to future data and warrant caution when evaluating claims of such generalization.
